topic.subject: social
topic.title: The revolt of 1857
topic.scope: causes, cartridges, Mangal Pandey, Meerut, Bahadur Shah Zafar, leaders at Kanpur, Lucknow, Jhansi, aftermath and Crown rule

misconceptions.statement: The British only came to India to spread Christianity.
misconceptions.why: Students often oversimplify complex economic and political motives into a single religious narrative.
misconceptions.fix: The British East India Company primarily aimed to maximize trade profits, secure resources, and establish political control over Indian territories.

probe.question: What was the primary reason the British East India Company expanded its control in India?
probe.wrong_answer: To convert all Indians to Christianity.

misconceptions.statement: All Indians were equally unhappy with British rule from the very beginning.
misconceptions.why: Textbooks often present a unified national front, ignoring that different sections of society had conflicting interests.
misconceptions.fix: Different groups like peasants, landlords, and kings had different grievances; some even benefited from British policies initially.

probe.question: Did every Indian support the revolt against the British?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, everyone in India hated the British equally and wanted them out immediately.

concepts.name: The immediate trigger: Cartridges and military unrest

misconceptions.statement: The revolt of 1857 was caused solely by the greased cartridges.
misconceptions.why: The dramatic nature of the cartridge incident is often highlighted in media and textbooks as the 'start' of the revolt.
misconceptions.fix: The cartridges were the immediate spark, but the revolt was the result of long-standing political, social, and economic resentment.

probe.question: Why did the sepoys revolt in 1857?
probe.wrong_answer: Because they were forced to use cartridges greased with cow and pig fat.

concepts.name: Spread of the revolt and regional leadership

misconceptions.statement: The revolt was a well-planned, coordinated war led by a single national leader.
misconceptions.why: Students project modern concepts of organized national movements onto the 19th-century revolt.
misconceptions.fix: The revolt was spontaneous and fragmented, with different local leaders like Rani Lakshmibai and Nana Saheb fighting for their own regional interests.

probe.question: Who was the commander-in-chief of the entire 1857 revolt?
probe.wrong_answer: Bahadur Shah Zafar planned and directed all the battles across India.

concepts.name: Aftermath and the transition to Crown rule

misconceptions.statement: After 1857, the British left India and gave power to the Indian kings.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the 'end of the Company rule' with the 'end of British rule'.
misconceptions.fix: The British government took direct control from the East India Company, making India a formal colony under the British Crown.

probe.question: What happened to British power in India after 1858?
probe.wrong_answer: The British government handed over the administration to Bahadur Shah Zafar.
